title: NGC 1872: open or globular cluster?
caption: The star cluster NGC 1872 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Large Magellanic Cloud, NGC 1872 · constellation Dorado · about 170000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Thousands of stars crowd NGC 1872, a rich star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy neighboring our own. This little-studied cluster lies in the constellation Dorado, the Dolphinfish, which is no relation of the dolphin and often appears on menus as mahi-mahi. Scottish astronomer James Dunlop probably spotted it first, in 1826, using a small telescope near Sydney, Australia.

Astronomers value clusters because their stars formed together, at the same time and place, so they share similar ages and starting compositions. Such studies have been vital for understanding how stars evolve, and Hubble extends them beyond the Milky Way to other galaxies of the Local Group.

Star clusters are usually called open or globular, but NGC 1872 shares traits with each type. Its richness matches a typical globular cluster, yet it is much younger, and like many open clusters it has bluer stars. Intermediate clusters like this are common in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.06 x 1.47 arcminutes) and distance (170000 light years), the frame spans roughly 151 × 73 light-years. Its light set out about 170,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the cluster through a yellow filter (F555W), shown in blue, and a near-infrared filter (F814W), shown in red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the individual stars of a cluster in another galaxy are far too faint to see without Hubble.
